questions.q: Which layer of the skin is derived from ectoderm and lacks its own blood vessels?
questions.explain: The epidermis is the avascular superficial stratified squamous epithelium derived from surface ectoderm, receiving nutrients by diffusion from dermal capillaries. The dermis lies beneath it and is vascularized.

open.q: Which layer of the skin originates from ectoderm and is avascular?

questions.q: Which layer of the skin lies immediately deep to the epidermis and consists largely of dense irregular connective tissue?
questions.explain: The dermis sits directly beneath the epidermis and contains dense irregular collagenous and elastic connective tissue that gives skin strength and elasticity. Subcutaneous tissue (superficial fascia) lies deep to the dermis.

open.q: Which skin layer lies immediately beneath the epidermis and consists primarily of dense irregular connective tissue?

questions.q: Why do surgical incisions made parallel to Langer cleavage lines tend to heal with less gaping and finer scars?
options: They align with the predominant orientation of dermal collagen bundles
questions.explain: Langer lines reflect the predominant direction of collagen fiber bundles in the reticular dermis. Incisions parallel to them separate rather than cut across tension lines, reducing wound retraction.

open.q: How do Langer cleavage lines relate to the collagen fibers in the dermis to reduce wound gaping?
accept: they follow the main direction of dermal collagen fibers

questions.q: Where in the human body is thick (glabrous) skin normally found?
options: Palms of the hands and soles of the feet
questions.explain: Thick glabrous skin covers the palms and soles, where mechanical friction and pressure are high, and features a thick stratum corneum without hair follicles. Most other body surfaces have thin hairy skin.

open.q: On which surfaces of the body is thick hairless skin typically located?
accept: palms of the hands and soles of the feet
glabrous skin of palms and soles

questions.q: Which skin appendage typically empties its lipid-rich secretion into a hair follicle rather than directly onto the skin surface?
questions.explain: Sebaceous glands are holocrine glands usually associated with hair follicles, releasing sebum into the follicular canal to lubricate hair and skin. Eccrine sweat glands open directly onto the skin surface via sweat pores.

open.q: Which cutaneous gland normally discharges its secretion into a hair follicle?

questions.q: What causes gooseflesh when a person is cold or frightened?
options: Contraction of arrector pili muscles pulling hair follicles upright
questions.explain: Arrector pili are small bundles of smooth muscle innervated by sympathetic fibers that attach to hair follicles and pull them upright, creating dimples (gooseflesh). Sweat glands do not produce gooseflesh.

open.q: Which muscles contract to produce gooseflesh by pulling hair follicles upright?

questions.q: Which type of sweat gland is widely distributed across most of the body and plays a primary role in thermoregulation via evaporation?
questions.explain: Eccrine sweat glands are abundant across general body skin (especially palms, soles, and forehead) and secrete watery sweat for evaporative cooling. Apocrine glands are restricted to specific regions such as the axilla and perineum.

open.q: Which sweat glands are widely distributed over most of the body and mainly aid thermoregulation?

questions.q: What is another standard anatomical term for the superficial fascia?
questions.explain: The superficial fascia is commonly called subcutaneous tissue or the hypodermis and consists of loose connective tissue and adipose tissue between the dermis and deep fascia. Deep fascia is a denser fibrous sheet investing muscles and deeper structures.

open.q: What is another name for the superficial fascia located between the dermis and deep fascia?

questions.q: Why does subcutaneous fat tend to accumulate more prominently in the superficial fascia of the lower abdomen, buttocks, and thighs?
options: Adipose tissue is stored there as an energy reserve and thermal insulator
Deep fascia is absent over those regions
Lymphatic drainage is blocked in those areas
Sebaceous glands are denser there than on the face
questions.explain: The superficial fascia serves as a major depot for fat storage, providing metabolic energy reserves, mechanical cushioning, and thermal insulation. Fat thickness varies with sex, age, and nutritional status rather than absence of deep fascia.

open.q: What are the main functional roles of fat stored in the superficial fascia?

questions.q: A patient with a lower abdominal wall laceration has fluid tracking downward over the pubis without entering the thigh. Which fascial layer in the lower anterior abdominal wall restricts this spread?
questions.explain: Scarpa fascia is the deeper membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the lower anterior abdominal wall and fuses with the deep fascia of the thigh (fascia lata) just below the inguinal ligament, limiting downward fluid spread into the thigh. Camper fascia is the superficial fatty layer.

open.q: Which membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the lower anterior abdominal wall limits fluid from spreading down into the thigh?

questions.q: In which region do striated muscle fibers (panniculus carnosus remnants) lie directly within the superficial fascia?
questions.explain: In the face and neck, muscles of facial expression and platysma develop in the superficial fascia, allowing them to pull on skin directly. In most other body regions, superficial fascia lacks striated muscle.

open.q: In which body regions do muscles such as platysma and muscles of facial expression lie within the superficial fascia?

questions.q: What is the primary structural characteristic of deep fascia compared with superficial fascia?
options: It is rich in loose fat lobules
It is a thin serous membrane
It is a dense, organized sheet of collagenous connective tissue
questions.explain: Deep fascia is a dense, relatively inelastic or organized sheet of collagen fibers that ensheathes muscles and forms fascial compartments. Superficial fascia is predominantly loose areolar and adipose tissue.

open.q: How does deep fascia differ structurally from superficial fascia?
accept: dense regular or organized collagenous tissue

questions.q: How do intermuscular septa and interosseous membranes formed from deep fascia help limb function?
options: They divide limbs into compartments and provide attachment surfaces for muscles
They secrete synovial fluid into adjacent joints
They conduct action potentials along peripheral nerves
They replace periosteum over long bone shafts
questions.explain: Deep fascia sends inward extensions (intermuscular septa) to bone that compartmentalize muscles with common actions and innervation, while broadening surface area for muscle attachment. Compartmentalization also influences how infection or hemorrhage spreads.

open.q: What two anatomical roles do intermuscular septa of deep fascia serve in the limbs?
accept: compartmentalize muscles and provide muscle attachment
divide compartments and give muscle attachment

questions.q: After a tibial fracture, swelling within a closed fascial compartment of the leg causes severe pain out of proportion and paresthesia. Why does unyielding deep fascia worsen this condition?
options: It dilates arterioles inside the compartment
It prevents outward expansion, raising intracompartmental pressure and compromising perfusion
It dissolves bone fragments into the bloodstream
It blocks lymphatic valves in the skin
questions.explain: Because deep fascia forms a tight, relatively non-expansile envelope around muscle compartments, rising edema or bleeding rapidly elevates compartment pressure above venous and capillary perfusion pressure, causing ischemia (compartment syndrome).

open.q: Why does tight deep fascia contribute to tissue ischemia when swelling occurs inside a limb compartment?
accept: it restricts expansion and increases compartment pressure
limits expansion and compromises blood flow
raises pressure and impairs blood supply

questions.q: Which localized thickening of deep fascia at the wrist holds flexor tendons close to the skeleton and prevents bowstringing?
questions.explain: Retinacula are localized bands or thickenings of deep fascia around joints such as the wrist and ankle that act as pulleys/straps to keep tendons in position during joint movement. The plantar aponeurosis supports the longitudinal arch of the foot.

open.q: Which thickened band of deep fascia at the wrist keeps flexor tendons in place during movement?

questions.q: In which region is deep fascia typically absent or poorly developed so that muscles can move freely without restriction?
questions.explain: Deep fascia is generally absent in the face, allowing muscles of facial expression to insert into skin and produce varied expressions without fascial restraint. In the limbs, deep fascia is well developed.

open.q: In which body region is deep fascia typically absent?

questions.sub: Vessels and nerves of skin and fascia
questions.q: How do veins in the superficial fascia assist venous return from the limbs during muscular activity?
options: Perforating veins connect superficial veins to deep veins compressed by contracting muscles
Superficial veins pump blood by intrinsic skeletal muscle contractions in their walls
Superficial veins carry oxygenated blood back to capillaries
Perforating veins bypass valves so blood flows solely outward
questions.explain: Superficial veins lie in the superficial fascia and communicate with deep veins via perforating veins equipped with valves directing blood inward. When deep muscles contract during movement, they squeeze deep veins and drive venous return upward.

open.q: How do perforating veins connect superficial fascia veins to the deep venous pump in limbs?
accept: they link superficial and deep veins and direct blood inward
connect superficial to deep veins with valves favoring inward flow
link superficial and deep venous systems

questions.sub: Vessels and nerves of skin and fascia
questions.q: Which type of nerve fibers carry pain, temperature, and light touch from the skin into the central nervous system?
questions.explain: Cutaneous nerves contain afferent sensory fibers conveying pain, temperature, and touch from skin receptors, along with sympathetic fibers to blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles. Somatic motor fibers supply skeletal muscles.

open.q: Which type of nerve fibers transmit touch, pain, and temperature signals from the skin?

questions.q: What is a dermatome?
options: A bundle of collagen fibers in the dermis
A localized thickening of deep fascia over a joint
An area of skin supplied predominantly by sensory fibers from a single spinal nerve root
A plexus of lymphatic vessels in the superficial fascia
questions.explain: A dermatome is the strip or area of skin innervated mainly by sensory axons from a single spinal nerve (dorsal root). Adjacent dermatomes overlap significantly, so cutting a single dorsal root usually causes partial sensory loss rather than total anesthesia.

open.q: What is the definition of a dermatome?
accept: skin area supplied by one spinal nerve root
area of skin innervated by a single spinal nerve
cutaneous region supplied by a single spinal nerve
skin territory of one spinal nerve root

questions.q: Why does division of a single spinal dorsal root often produce diminished sensation rather than complete loss of feeling in its dermatome?
options: Sympathetic fibers replace all lost touch receptors
The epidermis regenerates new nerve endings within hours
Deep fascia contains independent sensory ganglia
Adjacent dermatomes overlap in their sensory innervation
questions.explain: Neighboring dermatomes overlap substantially, meaning neighboring spinal nerves still supply part of the territory when one dorsal root is injured. Complete anesthesia in a dermatome typically requires injury to two or more adjacent roots.

open.q: Why is loss of sensation in a single dermatome usually incomplete after injury to one spinal nerve root?
accept: overlapping sensory supply from adjacent dermatomes

questions.q: Which layer of the skin has no blood vessels and receives nutrients by diffusion from the layer beneath it?
questions.explain: The epidermis is an avascular keratinised stratified squamous epithelium nourished by capillaries in the dermal papillae. The dermis is the vascular layer.

open.q: Which layer of the skin has no blood vessels and is nourished by diffusion from the dermis?

questions.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the deepest and contains the actively dividing cells?
questions.explain: The stratum basale rests on the basement membrane and contains the stem cells that replace the epidermis. Cells move outward and keratinise as they go.

open.q: Which is the deepest layer of the epidermis, where cell division occurs?

questions.q: Which thin, clear layer of the epidermis is found only in thick skin such as the palms and soles?
questions.explain: The stratum lucidum lies between the granulosum and the corneum in thick skin only. It is absent from thin skin.

open.q: Which thin, clear layer of the epidermis is present only in thick skin such as the palms and soles?

questions.q: Which epidermal cells produce melanin?
questions.explain: Melanocytes derive from neural crest and lie in the stratum basale. They transfer melanin granules to keratinocytes to protect against ultraviolet light.

open.q: Which epidermal cells, derived from neural crest, produce melanin?

questions.q: Which epidermal cells act as antigen-presenting cells?
questions.explain: Langerhans cells are dendritic cells of bone marrow origin that capture antigens and present them to T lymphocytes. Merkel cells are touch receptors.

open.q: Which cells of the epidermis capture antigens and present them to T lymphocytes?

questions.q: Which tissue forms the bulk of the reticular layer of the dermis?
questions.explain: The reticular layer is thick and made of dense irregular collagenous tissue. The papillary layer above it is loose areolar tissue.

open.q: What type of connective tissue forms the reticular layer of the dermis?

questions.q: Langer's lines (cleavage lines) correspond to the orientation of which structures?
options: Collagen fibre bundles in the dermis
questions.explain: Cleavage lines follow the predominant direction of dermal collagen bundles. They differ in direction in different parts of the body.

open.q: Langer's lines of the skin reflect the predominant direction of which dermal structures?

questions.q: The arrector pili muscles of hair follicles are supplied by which part of the nervous system?
questions.explain: Arrector pili are smooth muscle and contract with sympathetic stimulation, for example with cold or fear, causing goose bumps.

open.q: Which part of the autonomic nervous system supplies the arrector pili muscles?

questions.q: Eccrine sweat glands are supplied by sympathetic postganglionic fibres that release which transmitter?
questions.explain: Sweat glands are an exception in the sympathetic system because their postganglionic fibres are cholinergic. This is why anticholinergic drugs reduce sweating.

open.q: Which neurotransmitter do the sympathetic fibres supplying eccrine sweat glands release?

questions.q: What are the thickened bands of deep fascia that hold tendons in position at the wrist and ankle called?
questions.explain: Retinacula, such as the flexor and extensor retinacula, stop tendons from bowing away from the joint during movement.

open.q: What name is given to the thickened bands of deep fascia that hold tendons in place at the wrist and ankle?

questions.q: A manual labourer develops thick, hard calluses on the palms. Which epidermal layer is mainly thickened?
questions.explain: Repeated friction stimulates proliferation and keratinisation, thickening the stratum corneum, the outer layer of dead keratinised cells.

open.q: A manual labourer develops thick, hard calluses on the palms. Which epidermal layer is mainly thickened?

questions.q: A surgeon wants an incision to heal with minimal gaping and a fine scar. How should the incision be oriented relative to Langer's lines?
options: At random, as orientation does not matter
questions.explain: Incisions parallel to the cleavage lines cut fewer collagen fibres and gape less. Incisions across the lines are pulled open and tend to leave wide or keloid scars.

open.q: A surgeon wants an incision to heal with minimal gaping and a fine scar. How should it be oriented relative to Langer's lines?
accept: In line with the skin tension lines

questions.q: A superficial partial-thickness burn destroys the epidermis and upper dermis but heals without grafting. From which structures does the new epithelium regenerate?
options: Epithelium of hair follicles and sweat glands
questions.explain: Epithelial cells in the deeper parts of hair follicles and sweat gland ducts survive in the dermis and migrate out to resurface the wound. In a full-thickness burn these appendages are destroyed.

open.q: A superficial partial-thickness burn destroys the epidermis and upper dermis but heals without grafting. From which structures does the new epithelium regenerate?
accept: Hair follicles and sweat gland remnants

questions.q: After a tibial fracture a patient has a tense, swollen leg with severe pain on passive stretching of the toes. Which anatomical feature mainly allows the raised pressure to damage the muscles?
options: Unyielding deep fascia enclosing the compartment
questions.explain: The deep fascia, intermuscular septa and interosseous membrane form closed compartments that cannot expand. Pressure rises, compromises perfusion and may need fasciotomy.

open.q: After a tibial fracture a patient has a tense, swollen leg with severe pain on passive stretching of the toes. Which anatomical feature enclosing the muscles stops the swelling from expanding?

questions.q: In rupture of the spongy urethra, extravasated urine spreads into the scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall but not into the thigh. Why does it not enter the thigh?
options: Colles fascia attaches to the iliac crest
Scarpa fascia is continuous with the fascia lata
The membranous layer of superficial fascia fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament
Camper fascia is absent in the thigh
questions.explain: Colles fascia of the perineum is continuous with Scarpa fascia of the abdomen. Scarpa fascia fuses with the fascia lata below the inguinal ligament, which blocks spread into the thigh.

open.q: In rupture of the spongy urethra, extravasated urine spreads into the scrotum, penis and lower abdominal wall but not into the thigh. Why does it not enter the thigh?
accept: Scarpa fascia attaches to the fascia lata
Membranous layer fuses with the fascia lata below the inguinal ligament

questions.q: A diabetic patient injects insulin by the subcutaneous route. Into which layer is the drug delivered?
questions.explain: The hypodermis (superficial fascia) lies deep to the dermis and contains fat and vessels. Absorption from it is slow and steady, unlike intramuscular injection.

open.q: A diabetic patient injects insulin by the subcutaneous route. Into which layer is the drug delivered?

questions.q: An adolescent has acne from blocked and inflamed pilosebaceous units. Which gland's secretion accumulates in the follicle?
questions.explain: Sebaceous glands open into hair follicles and secrete sebum by holocrine secretion. Blocked ducts with sebum and keratin lead to comedones and inflammation.

open.q: An adolescent has acne from blocked and inflamed hair follicle units. Which gland's oily secretion accumulates in the follicle?

questions.q: Stretch marks (striae) appear on the abdomen after pregnancy. Which layer of the skin is torn?
questions.explain: Rapid stretching ruptures collagen and elastic fibres in the dermis. The epidermis stays intact, so the scar shows through it.

open.q: Stretch marks (striae) appear on the abdomen after pregnancy. Which layer of the skin is torn?

questions.q: A middle-aged man has a progressive flexion contracture of the ring and little fingers with a thickened cord in the palm (Dupuytren contracture). Which structure is affected?
questions.explain: Dupuytren contracture is fibrosis and shortening of the palmar aponeurosis, the thickened central deep fascia of the palm. It pulls the fingers into flexion.

open.q: A middle-aged man has a progressive flexion contracture of the ring and little fingers with a thickened cord in the palm (Dupuytren contracture). Which structure is affected?

questions.q: A runner has heel pain that is worst with the first steps in the morning, and tenderness at the calcaneal attachment of a thick band on the sole. Which structure is inflamed?
questions.explain: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the plantar aponeurosis, the thickened deep fascia of the sole attached to the calcaneus. It supports the longitudinal arch.

open.q: A runner has heel pain that is worst with the first steps in the morning, and tenderness at the calcaneal attachment of a thick band on the sole. Which structure is inflamed?
